Sarah thinks it's dangerous to invest in today's biggest bets based on pedigree alone, without a point of view on the business:

"I was talking to one of our founders and explaining that the quality of their storytelling and their ability to make the company's bets legible to investors is obviously very important to their success. 

All of the capital is not research scientists. So it's on entrepreneurs to go explain their story. But it varies how much fundamental understanding there is.

There's a lot of proxying of judgment to pedigree, or to other legible signals like who's invested. And so the decision making is less fundamental.

I asked an extraordinarily good investor friend, and I was like, I don't understand, what is this company gonna be that would be big, explain it to me. 

And his explanation was essentially, do you know the quality of this person? 

I'm like, yes, I've known the quality of the person for eight years. But the technical theory and the business don't make sense to me.

People are making large scale research bets without any intuition for them, or without any opinion on them. 

Not having a point of view on the business besides the pedigree of the person is very dangerous."

Could the same computation that powers AI also secure a blockchain?

Miners are paid to secure networks through computation. AI providers are paid to produce useful outputs for customers.

Proof-of-Useful-Work (PoUW) attempts to combine the two by making useful computation part of mining.

Earlier designs struggled to make useful work verifiable, difficulty-adjustable, and tightly coupled to the chain. Recent progress has made PoUW more technically credible.

The bullish thesis is a flywheel between AI demand and blockchain security.

AI customers provide external revenue for compute providers. Token rewards can subsidize their costs, enabling lower prices, which may attract more demand and compute supply.

But AI demand does not automatically strengthen the blockchain. It only helps when useful work contributes directly to consensus and its revenue remains tied to participation in the canonical chain. Otherwise, providers may shift their compute elsewhere.

More customer revenue reduces reliance on token rewards, allowing the AI business to grow without creating equivalent demand for the token. Token emissions can also bootstrap a compute market that would not survive on customer demand alone.

PoUW becomes a flywheel only if AI demand strengthens the blockchain and can replace token subsidies without pulling compute away from security.

in crypto, we often talk of 'impermanent loss' in the context of constant product swaps but ive been thinking recently about what might be the nature of 'permanent loss' and its associated hedges in comparison-

the mathematical intuition behind integrated var swap hedging techniques ultimately use the idea of replicating an infinite strip of options weighted by 1/K^2, and the practical idea here of course is that nothing is permanent if you can dynamically hedge for expected outcomes with weights (ie weigh likely events higher than unlikely events). what that means is you really need two variables to define what is impermanence itself - 1) energy (for the asset to move), and 2) time (for movement happens across the dimension of time)

in that system then, the nature of permanent loss must originate from the discrete recognition that it happens when there is either no energy or no time. And that makes sense because physics teaches you energy = power/time, and so it must mean power is zero (and sadly zero bound conditions are inherently unhedgable). though could it also mean infinite? might the answer lie in that the quality of permanence also happen via infinity, and if so is there a hedging technique that is possible?

as humans, the only variable we really have control over is time because time, unlikely energy (which is fixed), is relative. so time is both amazing and frustrating because we can perceive it differently based on our own frame of mind. for example, there are two ways you can lose track of time: the first is when you are fully alive living in the moment of extreme experience, and the second is when you are in a state of complete stillness, a trance of ennui. both are moments when you lose sense of time. when time is either zero or infinite.

as we get older, its easier to fall into the latter than the former: the constant routines of the daily commute, the daily tasks associated with children, the repetitive milestones of anniversaries and earnings calls, the P&L by fiscal calendars. but these are all traps of the brain that make time flat in the wrong way. that is when time becomes zero

the hedge against permanent loss then is to seek infinity by active living. to keep taking as many 'firsts' as possible (even if each first may be the last), to dance more, risk more, to feel the highest peaks of joy and troughs of sadness, to be alive. to make time feel infinite

the hedge to permanent loss therefore exists in the seams of moments to find infinity. some people access this via religion, others via drugs, etc but the truth is i'm not sure i personally have really found my own strategy nor asked myself very deeply. bitcoin can feel like a religion and a drug, but it doesn't really provide a sense of infinity (perhaps by design!). as i think about how volatile the macro world is becoming that is further distorting our sense of living in the moment, perhaps its time to dedicate some space to actively finding out what that means, to find a permanent hedge for the impermanence of life. i think its a worthy pursuit and tribute for the people that came before us, and the people that will be here after us

Adam --

Think of bitcoin as a service.  The service it provides is the ability to store wealth in a digital format without a government or a bank.

We are all used to services having value. For instance: Microsoft offers a service; the ability to edit Word and Excel documents, access cloud compute, etc.  The more people who want that service, the more valuable Microsoft is; the fewer people who want it, the less value Microsoft is; if no one wanted it, the value would be zero.

The same is true of bitcoin. 

The difference is, Microsoft is a company. To access its service, you can pay a fee to Redmond. Those fees are aggregated and paid out in dividends.

Bitcoin is not a company. The only way to access its service is to buy the asset. If you buy the asset, you get the service.

Your (eminently reasonable) criticism is that you don't like the service bitcoin provides.  But millions of people do.

I think if you frame it as a "service" you can get close to the debate of its future value.  Will more or fewer people want a digital way to store wealth that doesn't rely on a government or a bank in the future. I suspect the answer is more, but we will see!

Early on, I had to confront some major weaknesses. I have a terrible rote memory—I can't remember anything that doesn't have a clear reason for being what it is. Because of that, I was a bad student and I hated school.

Details have always been a mess for me. To supplement my own shortcomings, I learned that I need to surround myself and work with people who are meticulous and detail-oriented.

Beyond that, my early audaciousness came with a lot of arrogance—until I got the shit kicked out of me enough times to learn fear.

But what I ultimately realized through that process is that your weaknesses don't really matter. What matters is recognizing them, finding the right people to compliment you, and learning from your mistakes.
#Principles #SelfAwareness #RadicalTruth #RayDalio

When I was younger, I played football. I joined five benchwarmers in a challenge against the 6 best athletes on the team.

We ran routes they weren’t expecting.

We lined up in ways that confused them.

And we humiliated them.

As cliché as it may sound, that moment taught me everything: Anything is possible. There is always a way. The underdogs always have a shot. Try anything.

In my VC career, I had a couple early investment wins that nobody expected. Same lesson, different stakes.

That's why I invest the way I do. That's why I back the founders other VCs pass on. They are underdogs. They are trying new possibilities.

All because I've SEEN the benchwarmers win. Again and again.

They can always surprise you.
